focus: Minimum-cost output and why the MC curve cuts the ATC curve at the bottom of the U

variants.q: Define the minimum-cost output. Draw a graph with a U-shaped average total cost (ATC) curve and an upward-sloping marginal cost (MC) curve, and use it to explain why MC must cross ATC exactly at the lowest point of ATC.
variants.a:
Definition: the minimum-cost output is the quantity of output at which average total cost is lowest, the bottom of the U-shaped ATC curve (point M).

Graph: Q on the x axis, cost per unit on the y axis. Draw a U-shaped ATC and a rising MC that cuts ATC at its bottom M. On the falling part of ATC mark A1 → A2, with the MC of the next unit (MCL) below ATC. On the rising part mark B1 → B2, with MCH above ATC.

  • If MC < ATC, the next unit costs less than the average, so ATC falls (A1 → A2).
  • If MC > ATC, the next unit costs more than the average, so ATC rises (B1 → B2).
  • ATC stops falling and starts rising only where MC = ATC. So MC passes through the minimum of ATC, point M.

Example (Ben's Boots): 3rd pair MC $60 < ATC $78 → ATC falls to $72; 4th pair MC $84 > ATC $72 → ATC rises to $75. M = 3 pairs, $72.

variants.q: A bakery makes 9 cakes a day at an average total cost of $40 per cake. (a) The marginal cost of the 10th cake is $34. If the bakery makes 10 cakes, does ATC rise or fall? Find the new ATC. (b) The marginal cost of the 11th cake is $45. What happens to ATC now? Find it. (c) Which of 9, 10 or 11 cakes is the minimum-cost output? Explain with the MC–ATC rule.
variants.a:
(a) TC at 9 cakes = 9 × 40 = $360. MC ($34) < ATC ($40), so ATC falls. New TC = 360 + 34 = $394; new ATC = 394/10 = $39.40.

(b) MC ($45) > ATC ($39.40), so ATC rises. New TC = 394 + 45 = $439; new ATC = 439/11 = $39.91.

(c) ATC: 40 → 39.40 → 39.91. The lowest is $39.40, so the minimum-cost output is 10 cakes. Before 10, MC was below ATC (ATC falling); after 10, MC is above ATC (ATC rising). So ATC turns around at 10 cakes, where the MC curve crosses ATC.

variants.q:
True or false? Give a reason for each.

  1. If marginal cost is rising, average total cost must also be rising.
  2. At the minimum-cost output, marginal cost equals average total cost.
  3. If MC = $50 and ATC = $60, producing one more unit will raise ATC.
variants.a:
1. False. What matters is whether MC is above or below ATC, not whether MC is rising. MC can be rising but still below ATC, and then ATC keeps falling (Ben's Boots: MC rises 12 → 36 → 60 while ATC falls 120 → 78 → 72).
  2. True. ATC falls while MC < ATC and rises while MC > ATC, so it is lowest where MC = ATC. The MC curve crosses ATC at its bottom, point M.
  3. False. The new unit ($50) costs less than the average ($60), so it pulls the average down: ATC falls. ("For the average to be bigger, the new comer has to be greater than the average.")

focus: Short run vs long run, total product curve, marginal product and diminishing returns (f′(L) > 0, f″(L) < 0)

variants.q:
Define the short run and the long run. Then say whether each situation is short run or long run, and why:

  1. A plov café hires two extra cooks for the weekend, using the same kitchen.
  2. A car maker builds a second factory and hires 500 new workers over three years.
  3. A university adds more tutors next semester but cannot build new classrooms.
variants.a:
Short run: the time period in which at least one input is fixed. Long run: the time period in which all inputs can be varied. (It is about inputs, not a number of months.)

  1. Short run: the kitchen is fixed; only the cooks (variable input) change.
  2. Long run: both the factory (capital) and the workers change, so all inputs are varied.
  3. Short run: the classrooms are a fixed input; tutors are the variable input.

variants.q: A café has one kazan (fixed). With 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 cooks it makes 0, 40, 70, 90, 100, 105 plates of plov a day. (a) Find the marginal product of each cook. (b) Are there diminishing returns? Why? (c) Sketch the total product curve and describe its shape. (d) A 6th cook would leave output at 105 plates. What is his marginal product, and what does it mean for the TP curve?
variants.a:
(a) MPL = ΔQ/ΔL: 40 − 0 = 40; 70 − 40 = 30; 90 − 70 = 20; 100 − 90 = 10; 105 − 100 = 5.

(b) Yes. Holding the kazan fixed, each extra cook adds less: 40 > 30 > 20 > 10 > 5. Diminishing returns = marginal product is decreasing. The reason: more cooks share the same kazan.

(c) X axis: cooks (variable input); y axis: plates; the kazan is held constant. The curve rises (0, 40, 70, 90, 100, 105) but gets flatter, because each step up is smaller.

(d) MP of the 6th cook = 105 − 105 = 0. When MP = 0, total product stops rising: TP is at its top. (If MP became negative, TP would fall.)

variants.q:
True or false? Give a reason.

  1. "Diminishing returns" means that total output falls when the firm hires more workers.
  2. If the production function is Q = f(L) with f′(L) > 0 and f″(L) < 0, output rises with labor but more and more slowly.
  3. The long run means any period longer than one year.
variants.a:
1. False. Diminishing returns means the marginal product of an input falls when that input increases and other inputs are fixed. Total output can still rise, just by less each time (farm example: MPL 19, 17, 15 … 5, all positive).
  2. True. f′(L) is the slope of the TP curve = marginal product. f′(L) > 0: each extra worker adds output, so TP rises. f″(L) < 0: marginal product is falling, so TP gets flatter. This is diminishing returns.
  3. False. The long run is defined by inputs, not by time on a calendar: it is the period in which all inputs can be varied. The short run is when at least one input is fixed.

focus: Part 1 of Q21–Q22: the four cost curves (MC, AFC, AVC, ATC), their shapes, and why ATC is U-shaped (spreading effect vs diminishing returns effect)

variants.q: Sketch the family of cost curves for a firm like Ben's Boots. Name the four curves, give the formula for each, and describe the shape of each one.
variants.a:
Graph: quantity on the x axis, cost per unit ($) on the y axis.

  • MC = ΔTC/ΔQ (marginal cost): slopes upward. Increasing marginal cost, caused by diminishing returns to the variable input.
  • AFC = FC/Q (average fixed cost): always falling, because the same fixed cost is shared by more units.
  • AVC = VC/Q (average variable cost): rising.
  • ATC = TC/Q = AFC + AVC (average total cost): U-shaped.

MC cuts ATC at its lowest point M (Ben's Boots: 3 pairs, $72). The vertical gap between ATC and AVC is AFC, so it gets smaller as Q rises.

variants.q: A firm has fixed cost FC = $90. Its AVC at Q = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is $10, 20, 30, 40, 50. (a) Find AFC and ATC at each quantity. (b) For each step (1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5) say which effect wins: the spreading effect or the diminishing returns effect. (c) Use this to explain why ATC is U-shaped.
variants.a:
(a) AFC = 90/Q; ATC = AFC + AVC.

(b)

  • 1→2: AFC −45, AVC +10 → spreading wins, ATC falls (100 → 65).
  • 2→3: AFC −15, AVC +10 → spreading wins, ATC falls (65 → 60).
  • 3→4: AFC −7.50, AVC +10 → diminishing returns wins, ATC rises (60 → 62.50).
  • 4→5: AFC −4.50, AVC +10 → diminishing returns wins, ATC rises (62.50 → 68).

(c) At low output the fixed cost is spread over more units and AFC drops a lot, so ATC falls. Later AFC hardly falls, while each unit needs more variable input, so AVC rising dominates and ATC rises. Falling, then rising = U-shape (bottom at Q = 3, ATC = $60).

variants.q:
True or false? Give a reason.

  1. The AFC curve is U-shaped, like the ATC curve.
  2. The vertical distance between the ATC curve and the AVC curve gets smaller as output rises.
  3. The MC curve slopes upward because of the spreading effect.
variants.a:
1. False. AFC = FC/Q always falls: the same fixed cost is divided by more units (Ben's Boots: 108, 54, 36, 27 …). It never turns up.
  2. True. ATC = AFC + AVC, so ATC − AVC = AFC. AFC keeps falling, so the gap shrinks (Ben's Boots: 108 at 1 pair, only 10.80 at 10 pairs).
  3. False. MC slopes up because of diminishing returns to the variable input: with fixed equipment each extra worker adds less output, so each extra unit costs more. The spreading effect is about AFC falling.

focus: Part 2 of Q21–Q22: why MC crosses ATC (and AVC) at its lowest point M, the derivative proof, and Ben's Boots' minimum-cost output

variants.q: Prove that the MC curve crosses the ATC curve at the minimum of ATC. Use the derivative of ATC = TC/Q, and explain the result in words.
variants.a:
ATC = TC/Q. Using the quotient rule (and dTC/dQ = MC):

dATC/dQ = (MC·Q − TC)/Q2 = (1/Q)(MC − TC/Q) = (1/Q)(MC − ATC)

Since 1/Q > 0, the slope of ATC has the same sign as MC − ATC:

  • MC < ATC → slope < 0 → ATC falling.
  • MC > ATC → slope > 0 → ATC rising.
  • MC = ATC → slope = 0 → ATC at its minimum.

In words: a new unit below the average pulls the average down, a new unit above it pulls the average up. So ATC is lowest exactly where MC = ATC (point M). The same proof with VC instead of TC shows MC also crosses AVC at its minimum.

variants.q:
Use the formula dATC/dQ = (1/Q)(MC − ATC). For each firm, find the slope of ATC and say whether the firm is to the left of, to the right of, or at its minimum-cost output.

  1. Q = 10, MC = $30, ATC = $45.
  2. Q = 20, MC = $70, ATC = $55.
  3. Q = 15, MC = $50, ATC = $50.
variants.a:
1. dATC/dQ = (1/10)(30 − 45) = −15/10 = −1.5. Negative: ATC is falling (MC below ATC), so the firm is to the left of its minimum-cost output.
  2. dATC/dQ = (1/20)(70 − 55) = 15/20 = 0.75. Positive: ATC is rising (MC above ATC), so the firm is to the right of its minimum-cost output.
  3. dATC/dQ = (1/15)(50 − 50) = 0. MC = ATC, so ATC is at its minimum: the firm is at its minimum-cost output (point M).

variants.q: In Figure 7-8 for Ben's Boots, MC crosses ATC at point M. ATC at 2, 3, 4 pairs is $78, $72, $75, and the MC of the 3rd and 4th pairs is $60 and $84. (a) What is the minimum-cost output and the ATC there? (b) Use the MC numbers to show that ATC falls before M and rises after M. (c) Which other average cost curve does MC cross at its minimum?
variants.a:
(a) Minimum-cost output = 3 pairs, minimum ATC = $72 (point M).

(b) 3rd pair: MC $60 < ATC(2) $78, so the new unit pulls the average down: ATC falls to (156 + 60)/3 = $72. 4th pair: MC $84 > ATC(3) $72, so the new unit pulls the average up: ATC rises to (216 + 84)/4 = $75. ATC falls while MC is below it and rises while MC is above it, so MC crosses ATC at the bottom, M.

(c) The AVC curve. By the same average rule (and the same proof with VC), MC = AVC at the lowest AVC. At Ben's, MC of the 1st pair ($12) = AVC at 1 pair ($12), and after that MC is above AVC, so AVC only rises.
